title: Laying solid wood parquet floor tiles in adhesive
subtitle: Set out, glue, and bed small solid-wood parquet blocks in a herringbone or basket-weave pattern on a prepared concrete subfloor
excerpt: How to lay solid wood parquet blocks using a floor adhesive on a concrete subfloor. Covers acclimatisation, setting-out the pattern, spreading adhesive, bedding blocks, and sanding and finishing.
sourceNotes: Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (referenced, not reproduced). UK Flooring Alliance guidance notes for solid wood installation (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A small rectangular or square piece of solid hardwood (typically oak, pine, or beech), typically 230 x 70 mm and 18-22 mm thick, designed to be laid in geometric patterns. Older blocks are plain-sawn and finger-jointed; modern versions are often end-grain or engineered.

Leaving timber flooring in the room where it will be installed for several days before laying, so the moisture content of the wood stabilises to match the room conditions. Prevents buckling or gapping after installation.

A floor pattern in which rectangular blocks are laid at 45 degrees to the room, with each block at 90 degrees to the ones beside it, creating a V-shaped zigzag. Used for parquet and brick floors. Requires a diagonal set-out from the centre of the room.

content.text: Solid wood parquet is a block-by-block floor, glued directly to a concrete subfloor. The

or basket-weave pattern is set out from the centre of the room. Once the adhesive goes down, pace is important: the blocks must be bedded before the adhesive skins. Plan the whole setting-out first, spread in manageable sections, and bed methodically.
Acclimatise the blocks and prepare the subfloor

requirement comes first: leave unopened packs in the room for at least 3 days. The concrete subfloor must be flat (no deviation greater than 3 mm over 1.8 m), dry (moisture content below 75% RH or 2.5% by weight), and clean. Grind down any high spots and fill low spots with a floor-levelling compound. A damp subfloor will cause the blocks to cup or lift; test with a moisture meter or a polythene sheet taped down for 48 hours.

Find the centre of the room by snapping chalk lines between the midpoints of opposite walls. For herringbone, the setting-out line runs diagonally at 45 degrees to the room. Lay one dry run of the first few rows along the setting-out line to check the pattern works and to see what the edge cut will be at the walls. Adjust the setting-out point so the border cut is no narrower than half a block width. Mark the setting-out line clearly.
Spread adhesive and bed the blocks

Spread the adhesive with a notched trowel according to the adhesive manufacturer's specification. Most solid-block adhesives require a B2 or B3 notched trowel (2 mm or 3 mm notch). Work in sections of no more than 0.5 square metres at a time. Place each

firmly onto the adhesive and tap it down level with a rubber mallet. Maintain the pattern alignment as you work away from the setting-out line. Wipe adhesive off the face of the blocks immediately with the solvent recommended by the adhesive maker; dried adhesive is difficult to remove once set.

Allow the main field to cure overnight before cutting and fitting the border blocks. Measure and cut each border piece individually; rooms are rarely perfectly square and the gap varies. Leave a 10 mm expansion gap around the entire perimeter. Cut with a tenon saw or crosscut hand saw; a fine-tooth blade reduces splintering on the face side. Glue the border blocks individually, pressing them against the main field.

Allow 24 hours after the last block is laid before sanding. Hire a drum sander for the main area and an edge sander for the perimeter. Sand in three passes: coarse (36-grit to level the blocks), medium (60-grit), fine (100-grit). Vacuum and tack-cloth between passes. Apply two coats of hard-wax oil or three coats of polyurethane floor lacquer according to the product instructions. Sand lightly between coats with 180-grit. Cover the expansion gap with a matching hardwood bead fixed to the skirting.

attrs.symptom: Blocks cup upward at the edges after a few weeks
attrs.cause: The subfloor moisture content was too high at the time of laying, or the blocks were not acclimatised.
attrs.fix: Lift the affected blocks, allow the subfloor to dry thoroughly (use a dehumidifier), then relay on fresh adhesive.

attrs.symptom: Pattern loses alignment midway through the room
attrs.cause: The setting-out line was not extended far enough, or individual blocks crept during bedding.
attrs.fix: Use a long straight edge to check alignment every six to eight rows. Adjust the position of the next block back to line before the adhesive sets.

attrs.symptom: Adhesive squeeze-up stains the block faces
attrs.cause: Too much adhesive applied or the notch too coarse.
attrs.fix: Clean with the solvent specified by the adhesive maker while wet. Dried adhesive may need a cabinet scraper or careful use of a heat gun.
